en: To trick or mislead.

deceive.ety: From Middle English deceyven, from Anglo-Norman deceivre, from Latin dēcipiō (“to deceive; beguile; entrap”), from dē- (“from”) + capiō (“to seize”); see captive. Compare conceive, perceive, receive. Displaced native Old English beswīcan.

ex.en: Try it I think you will be deceived.
ex.ja: 騙されたと思ってやってみて。

ex.en: The boy I thought was honest deceived me.
ex.ja: 正直だと思っていた少年が私をだました。

ex.en: He is the last man to deceive me.
ex.ja: 彼は決して私をだますような人間ではない。

note.ja: de（離れて）+ ceiv（つかむ）+ e。（人の判断を）つかんで離さない →「だます・欺く」。deception（欺き）。

en: Someone who is detained, especially in custody or confinement.
Nervous, apprehensive.
Creatively challenging; cutting edge; leading edge.

edgy.ety: From edge + -y. Compare German eckig (“angular, edgy”).

ex.en: My boss is starting to get edgy.
ex.ja: 上司はいらいらしてきました。

en: A brief extra performance, done after the main performance is complete.
A call or demand (as by continued applause) for a repeat performance.
Please perform again!
To call for an extra performance or repetition of, or by.
To call for an encore.

encore.ety: Borrowed from French encore (“more, again”), and once used in this sense.

ex.en: Everyone called out to the singer for an encore.
ex.ja: 歌手に向かって盛んなアンコールが起こった。

ex.en: The pianist played two encores.
ex.ja: そのピアニストはアンコールに応えて２曲弾いた。

note.ja: フランス語で「もう一度」。英語では「アンコール」の意味で使う（フランスでは bis と言う）。

en: Extremely, greatly: to an enormous degree.
Shockingly.

enormously.ety:
Etymology tree
English enormous
Middle English -ly
English -ly
English enormously
From enormous + -ly.

ex.en: The economy of Japan has grown enormously.
ex.ja: 日本の経済は、大きく成長した。

ja: 誤る（To err is human：過ちは人の常）

en: To make a mistake.
To sin.
Elongated form of er (“sound of hesitation”).

err.ety: From Middle English erren, from Old French errer (“to wander, err, mistake”), from Latin errō (“wander, stray, err, mistake”, verb), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ers- (“to be angry, lose one's temper”). Cognate with Old English eorre, ierre (“anger, wrath, ire”), Old English iersian (“to be angry with, rage, irritate, provoke”), Old English ierre (“wandering, gone astray, confused”).

ex.en: He that thinks little, errs much.
ex.ja: あまり考えない者が、多くの過ちをおかす。

ex.en: He that talks much, errs much.
ex.ja: 多弁の人は多く誤る。

ex.en: I prefer to err on the side of caution.
ex.ja: 慎重にやって失敗するくらいのほうがいい。

note.ja: ラテン語 errare（さまよう・誤る）から。「誤る」。error、erratic と同じ。

en: To eject something violently (such as lava or water, as from a volcano or geyser).
To burst forth; to break out.

erupt.ety: From Latin eruptus, past participle of ērumpō (“to break out (of), to burst out (from)”), from e (“out”) + rumpō (“to break”).

ex.en: The volcano erupted suddenly, killing many people.
ex.ja: その火山は突然噴火し、多くの人が亡くなった。

ex.en: The volcano has erupted twice this year.
ex.ja: その火山は今年２度噴火した。

ex.en: The volcano may erupt at any moment.
ex.ja: その火山はいつなんどき爆発するかもしれない。

note.ja: e（外へ）+ rupt（破る）。破って外へ出る →「噴火する・爆発する」。

en: A concentrated coffee beverage brewed by forcing hot water under high pressure through finely ground coffee.
A drink that includes espresso as an ingredient.

espresso.ety:
Borrowed from Italian espresso, from caffè espresso (“pressed-out coffee”), form of esprimere (“to press out”), from Latin exprimere, from ex- (“out”) + primere (“to press”).
Some sources derive the term from "expressly" ("individually, directly") made for the customer, or from the Italian espresso ("fast"), as in the English word express ("fast"), although these explanations are not widely accepted. The original term for modern espresso (coffee extracted under pressure) was cream coffee, from Italian caffè crema (variant: crema caffè), due to the crema, and appeared on early Gaggia machines,

ex.en: An espresso doppio to drink inside.
ex.ja: エスプレッソドピオ店内で。

ex.en: I drank a very hot double espresso at the coffee shop this morning.
ex.ja: 今朝、コーヒーショップでとても熱いダブルエスプレッソを飲んだ。

note.ja: イタリア語 caffè espresso（押し出されたコーヒー）から。express と同じ。

en: To get away from by cunning; to avoid by using dexterity, subterfuge, address, or ingenuity; to cleverly escape from.
To escape; to slip away; — sometimes with from.

evade.ety: From Middle French évader, from Latin ēvādō (“to pass or go over; flee”), from ē (“out of, from”) + vādō (“to go; walk”). See also wade.

ex.en: Jack tried to evade paying his taxes.
ex.ja: ジャックは脱税しようとした。

ex.en: He was accused of evading tax.
ex.ja: 彼は脱税で非難された。

ex.en: We won't be able to evade punishment this time.
ex.ja: 今度は罰をまぬがれまい。

note.ja: e（外へ）+ vadere（行く）。「抜け出す」→「避ける」。evasion、invade と同じ。

en: Resembling a freak.
Incapable of producing results, useless; doomed not to be successful; not worth attempting.
Insignificant; frivolous.

futile.ety: Borrowed from Middle French futile, from Latin fūtilis.

ex.en: It isn't futile to go to university.
ex.ja: 大学へ行くことは無駄ではない。

note.ja: ラテン語 futilis（漏れやすい）から。fundere（注ぐ）の仲間。注いでもこぼれる →「無駄な・むなしい」。

en: The embryo of a seed, especially of a seed used as a cereal or grain. See Wikipedia article on cereal germ.
The small mass of cells from which a part of an organism develops, or a macroscopic but immature form of that part; a bud.
To germinate.

germ.ety: From Middle French germe, from Latin germen (“bud, seed, embryo”). Doublet of germen.

ex.en: Germs are too tiny for our eyes to see.
ex.ja: 細菌は小さすぎて我々の眼には見えない。

ex.en: This milk is free from germs.
ex.ja: この牛乳は殺菌してある。

ex.en: This chemical will prevent germs from breeding.
ex.ja: この化学薬品は細菌の繁殖を防ぐだろう。

note.ja: ラテン語 germen（芽・種）から。「芽」→「細菌・萌芽」。germinate（発芽する）と同じ。German（ドイツ人）とは別語。

en: Of, or relating to glaciers.
Very slow.
A glacial period (colloquially known as an ice age).

glacial.ety: Borrowed from French glacial, from Latin glaciālis, from glaciēs (“ice”). The sense "slow" refers to the speed of actual glaciers, typically around 1 meter per day.

en: A specialized cell, group of cells, or organ of endothelial origin in the human or animal body that synthesizes a chemical substance, suc…
A structure resembling a gland, especially a lymph node.

gland.ety: Late 17th century borrowing from French glande, alteration of Old French glandre, from Latin glandulae (“throat glands, tonsils”), plural of glandula (“a little acorn”), from glāns (“an acorn”) + -ula (diminutive nominal suffix).

note.ja: ラテン語 glandula（小さなドングリ）から。glans（ドングリ）。形が似ていることから「腺」。

en: Not very illuminated; dim because of darkness, especially when appearing depressing or frightening.
Suffering from gloom; melancholy; dejected.
Someone or something that is gloomy or pessimistic.

gloomy.ety: From gloom + -y. Cognate with Saterland Frisian glumig (“dark, gloomy”).

ex.en: I got gloomy and thought of giving up.
ex.ja: 私は落ち込んでしまいあきらめようかと思った。

ex.en: The room was gloomy and cold.
ex.ja: 部屋は薄暗くてひんやりしていた。

ex.en: There are a lot of gloomy sentences today.
ex.ja: 今日は、悲観的な文章が多いね。

note.ja: gloom（薄暗さ・憂鬱）+ -y。「薄暗い・憂鬱な」。

en: Having or showing grace in movement, shape, or proportion.
Magnanimous, lacking arrogance or complaint; gracious.

graceful.ety: From Middle English graceful. By surface analysis, grace + -ful.

ex.en: How can I say things to sound graceful?
ex.ja: どう言えば、おしとやかに聞こえる？

ex.en: She is beautiful, and what is more, very graceful.
ex.ja: 彼女は美しいが、さらによいことには非常に上品だ。

ex.en: The lady has a graceful manner.
ex.ja: その婦人の態度はしとやかだ。

note.ja: grace（優美さ）+ -ful。ラテン語 gratia（好意・優美）。「優雅な」。

en: Something which causes grief.
A wrong or hardship suffered, which is the grounds of a complaint.

grievance.ety: From Old French grievance, from the verb grever (“to irritate; to bother; to annoy”) + -ance, equivalent to grieve + -ance.

note.ja: grieve（悲しむ）+ -ance。ラテン語 gravis（重い）。「重い気持ち」→「不満・苦情」。grief、grave と同じ。

Spirited; resolute; unyielding.

en: Overwhelming mental anguish or grief, especially that caused by loss or disappointment.

heartbreak.ety: From heart + break. Compare heartache § Etymology.

ex.en: It's not that I particularly love heartbreak, but I really like songs about heartbreak.
ex.ja: 別に失恋が好きなわけじゃないけど、失恋ソングはすごく好きなんだよね。

note.ja: heart（心）+ break（壊すこと）。「悲嘆・失恋」。

A fiction genre in which a heist is central to the plot; a work in such a genre.
To steal, rob, or hold up (something).

en: A member of a fictional race of small humanoids with shaggy hair and hairy feet.
A person of short stature.

hobbit.ety: Coined in its current sense by J. R. R. Tolkien in the 1930s, featured in the novels The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings. Jocularly etymologized by him as from a hypothetical Old English *holbytla (literally “hole-builder”), from hol (“hole”) + bytlan (“to build”) + -a (“-er”). Tolkien was possibly influenced by similar terms for house-sprites (probably from Hob, a hypocoristic form of Robert), or an isolated mention of hobbits (with hobgoblins following immediately afterwards) in a list of sprites and bogies from the 19th-century Denham Tracts.

note.ja: トールキンが『ホビットの冒険』（1937年）で作った語。

en: The back of a horse.
A ridge of sand, gravel, and boulders.
On the back of a horse.

horseback.ety: From Middle English horsebacke, horsebak, horsbak, equivalent to horse + back.

ex.en: A man on horseback came along the path.
ex.ja: 男が馬に乗ってその道をやってきた。

ex.en: He likes to go out on horseback.
ex.ja: 彼は馬に乗って出かけるのが好きです。

ex.en: I'd like to try horseback riding.
ex.ja: 乗馬をしたいのですが。

note.ja: horse（馬）+ back（背）。「馬の背」。

en: The provision of palliative care for terminally ill patients, either at a specialized facility or at a residence, and support for the fam…
A specialized facility or organization offering palliative care for the terminally ill.

hospice.ety: Borrowed from French hospice, from Old French hospise, from Latin hospitium (“hospitality, an inn”). Doublet of hospitium.

note.ja: ラテン語 hospitium（もてなし・宿）から。hospes（客）。巡礼者の宿 →「ホスピス」。hospital と同じ。

A direct line between two people, especially one between heads of state to be used in an emergency.
To communicate over a telephone hotline.

en: The act of inhibiting.
A personal feeling of fear or embarrassment that stops one behaving naturally.

inhibition.ety:
From Middle English inhibicioun, inhibicione from Old French inibicion, from Latin inhibitio.
Morphologically inhibit + -ion.

ex.en: Tom is truly free from inhibition.
ex.ja: トムって、本当に自由奔放ね。

ex.en: Tom lies without any inhibition.
ex.ja: トムは平気で嘘をつく。

note.ja: inhibit（抑える）+ -ion。in + habere（保つ）。「抑制・ためらい」。

en: A number that is not a fraction; an element of the infinite and numerable set {..., -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, ...}.

integer.ety: Borrowed from Latin integer (“whole”), from Proto-Italic *n̥tagros (“untouched”). Doublet of entier and entire. Related to English tact, thack, and thwack.

note.ja: ラテン語 integer（触れられていない→完全な）から。in（否定）+ teg（触れる）。欠けのない数 →「整数」。integrity（完全性・誠実さ）も同じ。

Of or pertaining to a linkage between multiple distinct academic disciplines or fields of study.

From inter- + disciplinary.

note.ja: inter（間）+ discipline（学問分野）+ -ary。「学際的な」。

en: Stopping and starting, occurring, or presenting at intervals; coming after a particular time span.
Existing only for certain seasons; that is, being dry for part of the year.

intermittent.ety: From Middle French intermittent, from Latin intermittens (“sending between”), from prefix inter- (“among, on”) + mittens (“sending”), from mittere (“to send”).

ex.en: It's been intermittent for 2 or 3 months.
ex.ja: 断続的ですが、もう２、３ヶ月になります。

note.ja: inter（間に）+ mittere（送る）+ -ent。「間をおいて送られる」→「断続的な」。mission と同じ mit。

en: The act of making timid or fearful or of deterring by threats; the state of being intimidated.

intimidation.ety: From intimidate + -ion. Compare French intimidation; perhaps modeled on it.

note.ja: intimidate（脅す）+ -ion。in + timidus（臆病な）。「臆病にさせること」→「脅し」。timid と同じ。

en: A recital or a second performance; a repetition.
A variation or version.

iteration.ety: From Latin iterātiō, from iterō. Morphologically iterate + -ion.

en: A precept; a succinct statement or observation of a rule of conduct or moral teaching.

maxim.ety: From Anglo-Norman maxime and Middle French maxime, from Late Latin maxima (“axiom”), noun use of the feminine singular form of Latin maximus (apparently as used in the phrase prōpositiō maxima (“greatest premise”)). Doublet of maxima.

ex.en: He worked in his favorite maxim.
ex.ja: 彼は自分のすきな格言をいれた。

note.ja: ラテン語 maxima（最大の命題）から。max（最大）。最も重要な言葉 →「格言・金言」。

en: Black bile, formerly thought to be one of the four "cardinal humours" of animal bodies.
Great sadness or depression, especially of a thoughtful or introspective nature.
Affected with great sadness or depression.
Suggestive of wistfulness or subdued emotion.

melancholy.ety: From Middle English malencolie, from Old French melancolie, from Ancient Greek μελαγχολία (melankholía, “atrabiliousness”) (from μέλας (mélas), μελαν- (melan-, “black, dark, murky”) + χολή (kholḗ, “bile”)), referring to the humour which ancient Hippocratic and later Galenic medicine associated with sadness and despondency. Compare the Latin ātra bīlis (“black bile”). The adjectival use is a Middle English innovation, perhaps influenced by the suffixes -y, -ly. Doublet of melancholia.

ex.en: Her words were filled with melancholy.
ex.ja: 彼女の言葉は憂鬱に満ちていた。

ex.en: We sensed a melancholy note in his voice.
ex.ja: 彼の声には憂鬱な調子が感じられた。

ex.en: He was overcome by a feeling of melancholy.
ex.ja: 彼は憂うつな感情に打ちのめされた。

note.ja: ギリシャ語 melas（黒い）+ kholē（胆汁）。黒胆汁が多いと憂鬱になると考えられた。

en: Uncomfortable, especially due to one's surroundings.
Lost; disoriented, put in the wrong place.

ex.en: It seems I have misplaced your last mail.
ex.ja: 最新のメールの保存場所を間違ってしまったようです。

ex.en: I seem to have misplaced my key last night.
ex.ja: 私は昨晩キーを置き忘れたらしい。

ex.en: I misplaced your blue pen.
ex.ja: あなたの青いペンがなくなってしまいました。

en: Covered in mist; foggy.
Dim; vague; obscure.

misty.ety: From Middle English misty, mysty, misti, from Old English mistiġ (“misty, dark”), from Proto-West Germanic *mistig (“misty”), equivalent to mist + -y. Cognate with Scots misty, mistie (“misty”), West Frisian mistich (“misty, foggy”), Dutch mistig (“misty, foggy”), German Low German mistig (“foggy”).

ex.en: It was cold and misty.
ex.ja: 寒くて霧がかかっていた。

ex.en: The girl disappeared in the misty forest.
ex.ja: その女の子が霧たちこめる森の中でなくなっちまった。

ex.en: I think that Misty has different feelings towards insects.
ex.ja: ミスティーさんは虫について違う感情があると思う。

note.ja: mist（霧）+ -y。「霧の深い・涙ぐんだ」。

en: An implement for washing floors or similar, made of a piece of cloth, or a collection of thrums, or coarse yarn, fastened to a handle.
A wash with a mop; the act of mopping.
To rub, scrub, clean or wipe with a mop, or as if with a mop.

mop.ety: From Middle English mappe (also as mappel), perhaps borrowed from Walloon mappe (“napkin”), from Latin mappa (“napkin, cloth”). Believed to be from a Semitic source, variously claimed as Phoenician or Punic (the latter by Quintilian). Compare Modern Hebrew מַפָּה (mapá, “a map; a cloth”) (shortened from מַנְפָּה (manpah, “fluttering banner, streaming cloth”)). Doublet of map, nape, and nappe.

ex.en: I promise I'll mop the floor tomorrow morning.
ex.ja: 明日の朝、床のモップがけをするって約束するよ。

ex.en: Have you mopped the kitchen floor yet?
ex.ja: 台所の床のモップ掛けって、もうやった？

ex.en: Have you already mopped the kitchen floor?
ex.ja: 台所の床のモップ掛けって、もうやった？

note.ja: 中英語 mappe から。ラテン語 mappa（ナプキン）とされる。map（地図）と同じ語源。

Relating or pertaining to groups, households or families involving persons with different or mixed ethnicities or races.

note.ja: nude（裸の）+ -ity。「裸」。

To arrange neatly; tidy up.

spruce.ety: From Middle English Spruce, an alteration of Pruce (“Prussia”), from Medieval Latin, from a Baltic language, probably Old Prussian; for more, see Prussia. Spruce, spruse (1412), and Sprws (1378) were terms for commodities brought to England by Hanseatic merchants (beer, wood, leather). The tree with this name was also believed to have been native to Prussia. The adjective and verb senses ("trim, neat" and "to make trim, neat") are attested from 1594, and originate with spruce leather (1466), which was used to make a popular style of jerkins in the 1400s that was considered smart-looking.

note.ja: Pruce（プロイセン）の変化形。プロイセンから来た木 →「トウヒ」、プロイセン製の革 →「こぎれいな」。

en: The energy and strength for continuing to do something over a long period of time; power of sustained exertion, or resistance to hardship…

stamina.ety: From Latin stāmina, plural of stāmen.

ex.en: I don't have the stamina needed to play sports like Tennis.
ex.ja: 私は体力がないので、テニスのようなスポーツができません。

ex.en: What you lack is stamina.
ex.ja: お前に足りないのは、持久力だよ。

ex.en: Sam doesn't have the stamina to finish a marathon.
ex.ja: サムにはマラソンを完走するだけの力がない。

note.ja: ラテン語 stamen（糸）の複数形。運命の女神が紡ぐ命の糸 →「生命力」→「スタミナ」。

en: Occurring in the part of our mind that we are not normally aware of.
The part of the mind that we are not normally aware of.

ex.en: Maybe the impulse was working upon her subconscious.
ex.ja: たぶん彼女の潜在意識の中にそういう衝動があったんでしょうね。

en: Pertaining to tension, especially of the muscles.
Restorative; curative; or invigorating.
A substance with medicinal properties intended to restore or invigorate.
Tonic water.

From Ancient Greek τονικός (tonikós), from τόνος (tónos). 17th century writers believed health to be derived from firmly stretched muscles, thus tonic; the extension of tonic medicine appeared in the late 18th century. By surface analysis, ton(e) + -ic.

ex.en: What do you need to make gin and tonic?
ex.ja: ジントニックを作るには何がいるの？

ex.en: I'd like a vodka and tonic.
ex.ja: ウォッカ・トニックをください。

ex.en: I'd like a gin and tonic.
ex.ja: ジン・トニックをください。

note.ja: ギリシャ語 tonikos（張りの）から。tonos（張り・音調）。「体に張りを与える」→「強壮剤」、音楽の「主音」。tone と同じ。

en: Causing trouble or anxiety.

ex.en: It is the first step which is troublesome.
ex.ja: 厄介なのは最初の一歩だ。

ex.en: In any case, it's troublesome, isn't it?
ex.ja: どっちにしても、厄介ですね。

ex.en: We have to somehow come through this troublesome situation.
ex.ja: 我々はこの難局を何とかして切り抜けなければならない。

note.ja: trouble（困難）+ -some（〜を生じる）。「厄介な」。

en: Commonwealth standard spelling of tumor.

tumour.ety: From Middle English tumour, from Old French tumour, from Latin tumor (“swelling”), from tumeō (“bulge, swell”, verb), from Proto-Indo-European *tewh₂- (“to swell”). Related to English thumb.

ex.en: I have fibroid tumours. Is there a way to stop them getting large?
ex.ja: 子宮筋腫があります。大きくならないようにする方法はありますか？

note.ja: tumor のイギリスのつづり。

en: A world in which everything and everyone works in perfect harmony.

utopia.ety:

Proto-Indo-European *-i-eh₂
Proto-Hellenic *-íā
Ancient Greek -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā)
New Latin Ūtopiader.
English utopia
From New Latin Ūtopia, the name of a fictional island possessing a seemingly perfect socio-politico-legal system in the book Utopia (1516) by Sir Thomas More. Coined from Ancient Greek οὐ (ou, “not”) + τόπος (tópos, “place, region”) + -ία (-ía). Compare English topos and -ia.

note.ja: トマス・モアの著書『ユートピア』（1516年）から。ギリシャ語 ou（ない）+ topos（場所）。「どこにもない場所」。

en: To become invisible or to move out of view unnoticed.
To become equal to zero.
The brief terminal part of a vowel or vocal element, differing more or less in quality from the main part.
A magic trick in which something seems to disappear.

vanish.ety:
Aphetic for obsolete evanish, from Middle English evanisshen, esvanisshen, from Old French esvanir, esvaniss- (modern French évanouir), from Vulgar Latin *exvanire (“to vanish, disappear, to fade out”), from Latin ēvānēscō, ēvānēscere, from vānus (“empty”). By surface analysis, Latin vān- + -ish (“verb suffix”). Doublet of evanesce.
Displaced native Old English cwincan, whose causative persists as quench (“put out (fire)”).

ex.en: The tiger is a vanishing species.
ex.ja: 虎は消滅しかかっている種族である。

ex.en: We should try to be philosophical about life; wealth gained could also vanish.
ex.ja: 人生はあきらめが肝心。設けた財産も消えさることがありうるのだから。

note.ja: ラテン語 vanescere（空になる）から。van（空の）。→「消える・消滅する」。vain、vacant も同じ祖先。

English -ly
English vigorously
From vigorous + -ly.

ex.en: He walked vigorously ahead of us.
ex.ja: 彼はわれわれの先をどんどん歩いて行った。

note.ja: vigorous（精力的な）+ -ly。「精力的に・激しく」。

en: In a visible manner; openly.

visibly.ety:
Etymology tree
English visible
Middle English -ly
English -ly
English visibly
From visible + -ly.

ex.en: He was visibly nervous.
ex.ja: 彼は目に見えて緊張していた。

ex.en: Tom was visibly nervous.
ex.ja: トムは目に見えて緊張していた。

note.ja: visible（見える）+ -ly。ラテン語 videre（見る）。「目に見えて」。

en: A body of water, such as a river, channel or canal, that is navigable.
A conduit or watercourse, such as on the deck of a ship, to drain water.

waterway.ety: From Middle English waterwey, from Old English wæterweġ (“waterway”), from Proto-West Germanic *watarweg, equivalent to water + way. Compare Saterland Frisian Woaterwai (“waterway”), West Frisian wetterwei (“waterway”), Dutch waterweg (“waterway”), German Wasserweg (“waterway”), Danish vandvej (“waterway”), Swedish vattenväg (“waterway”).

ex.en: The waterways branch out across the plain.
ex.ja: 平野を横切って水路が枝分かれしている。

ex.en: The waterways ramify across the plain.
ex.ja: 平野を横切って水路が枝分かれしている。

note.ja: water（水）+ way（道）。「水路」。

en: Land that is covered mostly with water, with occasional marshy and soggy areas.

wetland.ety: From wet + land. Cognate with West Frisian wetlân.

note.ja: wet（湿った）+ land（土地）。「湿地」。

en: Without notice to prepare the mind for the event; sudden; hasty; unceremonious.
Curt in manner.
To interrupt suddenly.
Something which is abrupt; an abyss.

abrupt.ety: First attested in 1583. Borrowed from Latin abruptus (“broken off”), perfect passive participle of abrumpō (“break off”), formed from ab (“from, away from”) + rumpō (“to break”).

ex.en: The car came to an abrupt stop.
ex.ja: その車は急停車した。

ex.en: The car made an abrupt turn.
ex.ja: その車は不意に方向を変えた。

ex.en: Excuse me for the abrupt question.
ex.ja: つかぬことをお伺いします。

note.ja: ab（離れて）+ rupt（破る）。ちぎれ離れた →「突然の・ぶっきらぼうな」。

zh: 首字母縮略詞 /首字母缩略词

en: Generally such abbreviations, including those pronounced as individual letters (initialisms such as "TNT").
Exclusively such abbreviations when pronounced as a word (as "laser" or "NATO").
To form into an acronym.

acronym.ety: Borrowed from German Akronym (from Ancient Greek ἄκρον (ákron, “end; peak”) + ὄνυμα (ónuma, “name”)), modelled after Homonym and Synonym, first attested in German in the early 1900s and in English in 1940. By surface analysis, acro- (prefix meaning ‘beginning; high’) + -onym (suffix meaning ‘name’)

note.ja: ギリシャ語 akron（先端）+ onyma（名前）。「頭の文字でできた名前」→「頭字語」。acrobat（つま先で歩く人）と同じ akro。

en: The state of adverse conditions; state of misfortune or calamity.
An event that is adverse; calamity.

adversity.ety: From Old French adversité, from Latin adversitātem, the accusative singular of adversitās, from adversus, the perfect passive participle of advertō (“to turn toward”).

ex.en: Adversity makes a man wise, not rich.
ex.ja: 艱難汝を玉にす。

ex.en: Adversity is the best school.
ex.ja: 逆境で人は成長する。

ex.en: They must have struggled against adversity from their early days.
ex.ja: 彼らは幼い時から逆境と闘ってきたにちがいない。

note.ja: ad（〜に）+ vers（向ける）+ ity。（運が）こちらに背を向けること →「逆境・不運」。

en: A signed document wherein an affiant makes a sworn statement.
To swear by such a document.

affidavit.ety: From Medieval Latin affidavit (“he has sworn”), the third person singular perfect tense of affido (“swear”), from fīdō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeydʰ- (“to command, to persuade, to trust”). Cognate to fidelity and faith (same Latin root), but not to affirm (shared Latin ad- prefix, but different Latin and Proto-Indo-European roots).

note.ja: 中世ラテン語で「彼は誓った」。affidare（誓う）。「宣誓供述書」。fidelity と同じ fid。

en: Divination about human affairs or natural phenomena from the relative positions of celestial bodies.

astrology.ety: From Middle French astrologie, and its source, Latin astrologia (“astronomy”), from Ancient Greek ἀστρολογία (astrología, “telling of the stars”), from ἄστρον (ástron, “star, planet, or constellation”) + -λογία (-logía, “treating of”), a combination form of -λόγος (-lógos, “one who speaks (in a certain manner)”). Morphologically astro- + -logy.

ex.en: Are you interested in astrology?
ex.ja: 星占いに興味ある？

ex.en: What's the difference between astronomy and astrology?
ex.ja: 天文学と占星学とは何が違うでしょう？

note.ja: astr（星）+ o + log（学問）+ y。星の学問 →「占星術」。astronomy（天文学）と区別。

en: A hill.
A mound of earth and stones raised over a grave or graves.

The total mass of all, or a specified category of, living things within a specific area, habitat, etc.

en: A shirt for women or girls, particularly a shirt with buttons and often a collar; a dress shirt tailored for women.
A loose-fitting uniform jacket.
To hang a garment in loose folds.
To tuck one's pants/trousers (into one's boots).

1828, from French blouse (“a workman's or peasant's smock”), see that for more.

ex.ja: 彼女はそのブラウスをすばやく洗った。

ex.ja: 彼女は赤いブラウスを着た。

note.ja: フランス語 blouse（仕事着）から。語源ははっきりしない。

en: A person or group of persons, often armed, responsible for protecting someone.
To act as bodyguard for (someone).
To protect (someone or something).

ex.en: What I need is a bodyguard.
ex.ja: 私に必要なのは、ボディガードです。

ex.en: Tom has a personal bodyguard.
ex.ja: トムには個人的なボディガードがいる。

ex.en: The bodyguard was wearing an earpiece.
ex.ja: ボディーガードは、イヤホンをしていた。

note.ja: body（体）+ guard（守る人）。「ボディーガード」。

en: One who borrows.

borrower.ety: From Middle English borower, borewer, borwere, equivalent to borrow + -er (agent suffix).

ex.en: Banks are cutting lending to industrial borrowers.
ex.ja: 銀行は産業向け貸出を減らしている。

note.ja: borrow（借りる）+ -er。「借り手」。

en: A branch of biology concerned with the scientific study of plants.
The plant life of a geographical area; flora.

botany.ety: First attested in 1696: Back-formation from botanic.

ex.en: Botany is the scientific study of plants.
ex.ja: 植物学とは植物の科学的研究のことである。

ex.ja: 植物学は植物の研究を扱っている。

ex.ja: 動物学と植物学は生命の研究を取り扱っている。

note.ja: ギリシャ語 botanē（草・牧草）から。boskein（家畜に草を食べさせる）。「植物学」。

en: The larva of a butterfly or moth; leafworm.
A vehicle with a caterpillar track; a crawler.
To move along slowly, drawing one's body up, in the manner of a caterpillar.

caterpillar.ety: From Middle English catirpel, catirpeller, probably from Old Northern French catepeluse (Modern French chatte + pileuse (“hairy cat”)), from Late Latin catta + pilōsa. ex.en: This caterpillar will become a beautiful butterfly.
ex.ja: この芋虫がきれいな蝶になるのだ。

ex.ja: この毛虫は、蝶々になるんだよ。

ex.en: The caterpillar turned into a butterfly.
ex.ja: 毛虫が蝶々に変わった。

note.ja: 古北フランス語 catepelose（毛の生えた猫）とされる。「毛虫」→ 毛虫のように進む →「キャタピラー」。

en: Talk, especially meaningless or unimportant talk.
The sound of talking.
To talk idly.
To make a noise by rapid collisions.

ex.en: Ah, I've chattered on too much, haven't I?
ex.ja: 喋りすぎてしまいましたね。

ex.en: The teacher told us to stop chattering.
ex.ja: 先生は私たちにおしゃべりするのをやめるよう言った。

ex.ja: おしゃべりはやめて仕事をすませなさい。

en: A member of a clergy.
A spellcaster class that receives their spells (especially healing) from their deity.
Of or pertaining to the clergy.

An instrument for compressing an artery (especially the femoral artery) or other part.

en: To grant as a possession; to bestow.
To talk together, to consult, discuss; to collogue.

confer.ety: From Early Modern English conferre, from Middle French conférer, from Old French conferer, from Latin cōnferō. ex.en: The university conferred its highest degree on him.
ex.ja: その大学は彼に最高の学位を授けた。

ex.ja: 私は困った時はいつでも彼に相談する。

ex.ja: あなたはこの問題を弁護士に相談するべきです。

note.ja: con（共に）+ fer（運ぶ）。（意見を）持ち寄る →「協議する」、（名誉を）運んで与える →「授与する」。

en: A wild feline, of species Puma concolor, native to the Americas.

cougar.ety: From French couguar, from Portuguese cuguardo, a deformation of Brazilian Portuguese suçuarana (earlier çuçuarana), from Old Tupi sûasuarana.

note.ja: トゥピ語（南米）に由来する。「ピューマ」。

To repeat the aforesaid, the earlier action etc.

ex.ja: あなたが言うのは「右に同じ」だけ、それは「愛してる」とは違う。

en: Growing further apart; diverging.
(said of a sequence or series) Diverging; not approaching a limit.

divergent.ety: From Latin dis- (“apart”) + vergere (“to turn”) + the adjectival suffix -ent.

en: The highest degree awarded by a university faculty.

Liberality of sentiment; breadth of view.

ex.ja: 彼は最近改宗したカトリック信者です。

en: A chemical element (symbol Co) with an atomic number of 27: a hard, lustrous, silver-gray metal.
Cobalt blue.

Doublet of kobold.

note.ja: ドイツ語 Kobalt（小鬼）から。鉱夫を悩ませた鉱石を小鬼のしわざと考えたことから。nickel と同じ発想。

en: One who compiles.
A computer program that transforms source code into object code.

compiler.ety: From Middle English compilour, from Anglo-Norman compilour, from Old French compileur, from Latin compīlātōrem, equivalent to compile + -er.

en: Wilderness where human development is prohibited.
A jam or thick syrup made from fruit and sugar.
To save for later use, sometimes by the use of a preservative.
To protect an environment, heritage, etc.

conserve.ety: From Middle English conserven, from Old French conserver, from Latin conservare (“to keep, preserve”), from com- (intensive prefix) + servo (“keep watch, maintain”). See also observe.

ex.en: We must try to conserve our natural resources.
ex.ja: 我々は天然の資源を保存するように勤めなければならない。

ex.en: He conserved his energy for the next game.
ex.ja: 彼は次の試合のために精力を蓄えた。

ex.en: Please conserve water during the summer.
ex.ja: 夏には節水して下さい。

note.ja: con（完全に）+ serv（保つ）+ e。そのまま保つ →「保存する・節約する」。

en: An arbitrary formation of stars perceived as a figure (especially one from mythology) or pattern, or a division of the sky including it, …
Any of the 88 regions of the sky officially recognized by the International Astronomical Union, including all stars and celestial bodies …

ex.en: Ancient astronomers noticed constellations and gave them names.
ex.ja: 古代の天文学者は、星座を見つけ、名前をつけた。

note.ja: con（共に）+ stella（星）+ -ation。「星の集まり」→「星座」。stellar と同じ。

en: An outline, boundary or border, usually of curved shape.
A line on a map or chart delineating those points which have the same altitude or other plotted quantity: a contour line or isopleth; (me…
To form a more or less curved boundary or border upon.
To mark with contour lines.

contour.ety: Borrowed from French contour, from contourner, equivalent to con- + tour.

note.ja: イタリア語 contorno（輪郭）から。con + tornare（回す）。「周りをなぞった線」→「輪郭・等高線」。turn と同じ。

en: Having a crisp texture; brittle yet tender.
The well-baked fat on the surface of a piece of roasted meat.

crispy.ety: From Middle English crispy (“crisped, curly”), equivalent to crisp + -y.

en: Any regulation requiring people to be off the streets and in their homes by a certain time.
A regulation requiring loud or disruptive activities such as concerts and sporting events to end by a certain time.

curfew.ety: From Middle English curfu, from Old French cuevre-fu (French couvre-feu), from the imperative of covrir (“to cover”) + fu (“fire”). Compare kerchief.

ex.en: Are you going to pull curfew on me?
ex.ja: 外出の時間制限をするつもりですか。

ex.en: The curfew is at 10 pm.
ex.ja: 門限は１０時です。

ex.en: What time is the curfew?
ex.ja: 門限何時？

note.ja: 古フランス語 cuevrefeu（火を覆え）から。夜に火を消す合図の鐘 →「夜間外出禁止令・門限」。cover + feu（火）。

en: In a manner which leaves little question; definitely, clearly.
In a decided or final manner; resolutely.

decidedly.ety:

From decided + -ly.

ex.ja: それは明らかに、満足すべきものとは言いがたい。

ex.en: Christi's mysteries are most decidedly interesting.
ex.ja: クリスティーの推理小説は断然面白い。

note.ja: decided（明白な）+ -ly。「明らかに・断然」。

en: An adamant belief in a falsehood despite incontestable evidence.
The state of being deluded or misled, or process of deluding somebody.

delusion.ety: Borrowed from Latin dēlūsiō. (This etymology is missing or incomplete. Please add to it, or discuss it at the Etymology scriptorium. Particularly: “a direct borrowing from latin or e.g. through french?”)

ex.en: That girl is under the delusion that she is a princess.
ex.ja: あの少女は自分が王女様だという妄想にとらわれている。

ex.en: People have worldly passions which lead them into delusions and sufferings.
ex.ja: 人には、迷いと苦しみのもとである煩悩がある。

note.ja: delude（だます）+ -sion。de + ludere（遊ぶ）。「もてあそばれること」→「妄想」。ludicrous と同じ。
